title: Nifty Down 13 Percent Faces Worst Year in Decade as Strategists Urge Caution
excerpt: Spark Capital says slowing growth, high crude and stretched valuations may cap returns despite expected 20% September-quarter profit growth, while brokerages see only a technical November rebound.
body:
• The Nifty 50 is down about 13% in 2026, on course for its worst annual performance in over a decade after nearly tripling over the previous 10 years.
  • Spark Capital told Reuters the slide may not yet be a buying opportunity, citing slowing growth, elevated oil prices and stretched valuations.
  • Brokerages see a possible technical rebound in November: IIFL puts the range at 23,300 to 23,500, Nuvama at 23,250 with a sustained rally needing a break above 23,480.
  • Spark expects September-quarter Nifty profit growth of 20%, the fastest in three years, but says future returns will depend on earnings delivery, not valuation re-rating.

India's Nifty 50 has fallen about 13% this year and is on course for its worst annual performance in over a decade, a decline that has left investors weighing whether lower prices are an entry point or a warning. Spark Capital Advisors, which has advised on more than $13 billion of private equity and merger transactions, argues the fall alone does not make the case to buy. Slowing growth, elevated oil prices and stretched valuations could limit returns, Thyagesh Baba, non-executive director at Spark Capital, told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday.

What has to go right next year

Baba set four conditions for a better outlook next year: sustained earnings growth, foreign investors returning after record outflows, easing crude prices, and a revival in private investment. He did not give a specific index target. Future returns, he said, will likely depend more on earnings delivery than on broad-based valuation gains, a shift after a decade in which the index nearly tripled.

On earnings, the near-term numbers are stronger than the index level suggests. Nifty 50 companies are expected to deliver 20% profit growth in the September quarter, their fastest pace in three years. Baba cautioned against extrapolating the old pace, saying investors accustomed to 20% to 25% annual earnings growth should recognise that 16% growth remains robust in an economy growing at 10% to 12% in nominal terms.

"The old model of borrowing at 18%-20% to fund businesses generating 11%-12% returns on capital has largely faded."

— Thyagesh Baba, Non-Executive Director, Spark Capital

Oversold in October, capped by crude

Trading desks see room for a bounce even if strategists stay cautious. The Hindu BusinessLine, reporting Reuters, said the Nifty briefly dipped into oversold territory in October, with its relative strength index below 30, and ended the October derivatives series virtually flat while mid-caps and small-caps lost about 4% each. IIFL Capital sees scope for a technical rebound to 23,300 to 23,500, but said only favourable announcements that revive foreign flows could trigger a sharp short-covering rally beyond 23,500. Nuvama described positioning for the November series as directionally inconclusive, with oversold conditions capable of lifting the index toward 23,250 and a sustained rally requiring a decisive break above 23,480.

Foreign positioning has softened at the margin. Investors cut Nifty index short positions to 221,000 contracts at the end of the October series from 267,000 at the start, added long contracts in single-stock futures and reduced index futures open interest, according to Nuvama. That shift points away from aggressive bearishness, not yet toward conviction buying. Global flows are a second constraint: while Indian markets were flat in October, MSCI's emerging markets index slid 7.4% as investors reconsidered AI bets amid high valuations, and money continued to chase AI-linked markets.

Oil remains the domestic vulnerability. As the world's third-largest crude importer, India faces higher inflation, strain on public finances and pressure on corporate profits when crude stays elevated. In October, a 16.3% surge in information technology stocks after better-than-expected results helped benchmarks offset oil-driven losses, which IIFL called the only silver lining in the series. Nuvama sees added bullish positions in IT and telecom for November, with defensive positioning in metals, autos and FMCG.

The case for patience

Spark's longer-term view is not bearish on the economy itself. Baba pointed to a healthier banking system after years of regulatory tightening, lower corporate leverage and more disciplined capital allocation. Spark's Midas fund focuses on companies one to three years before listing rather than late-stage pre-IPO premiums, and Baba expects private credit, backed by cash flows, to play a larger role in portfolios. For an investor deciding between buying now and waiting, the combined message from strategists and brokerages is narrow: a technical rebound is plausible in November, but a durable re-rating needs earnings to hold, crude to ease and foreign money to return. Until those conditions line up, the 13% fall is a cheaper market, not yet a confirmed opportunity.
